newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: FOCUS-S.Korea trade surplus raises economy hopes.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-S.Korea trade surplus raises economy hopes.

text.p: South Korea in June registered its first monthly trade surplus since December 1994, triggering broad optimism that the country's economy had turned the corner.
The surplus news also sent the Seoul stock market to a sharply higher close on Tuesday, brokers said. The composite stock index closed up 12.63 points, or 1.69 percent, at 758.03.
The trade ministry said on Tuesday the customs-cleared trade balance turned to a $97.6 million surplus in June from a $426 million deficit a year earlier.

"I expected the trade deficit to shrink considerably from this summer on," said Steve Marvin, head of research at Ssangyong Investment Securities. "I think this would become a trend for the rest of the year."

He said a blowout in the trade account last year because of a collapse in prices of major export items and a rise in import costs made the comparable figure this year look better. Moreover, both figures had begun to stabilise, he said.
"We are at the bottom of an economic cycle and the economy will do better in the second half than in the past 12 months," Marvin said.
Lee Jung-ja, research head at HSBC James Capel, agreed.
"It shows signs that the economic slump is bottoming out," she said. "The trade balance is improving on the back of weak imports and a halt in falling export prices."
South Korea's exports rose 9.2 percent to $12.3 billion in June, marking the third straight monthly rise for 1997.
Imports gained 4.4 percent to $12.2 billion in June.
The ministry said South Korea's customs-cleared trade deficit totalled $9.36 billion in the first half of this year, up from $8.07 billion in the same period of 1996.
The monthly surplus also compared to a shortfall of $613 million in May, the figures showed.
"A rise in semiconductor exports and growth in sales of petrochemical and steel products prompted the increase in exports," the ministry said.
Semiconductor sales abroad gained 27.3 percent in June, while exports excluding computer chips rose 6.9 percent.
The ministry said imports rose last month despite a 3.3 percent fall in May because comparable import figures for June last year were relatively low.
It said imports of capital goods posted firm growth of 21.5 percent in June on signs of an economic recovery.
However, imports of consumer materials slipped for the second consecutive month in June because a decline in international grain prices and slowing corn imports.
The ministry said it was too early to predict a bullish trend despite the June surplus.
"Imports of capital goods could increase in the second half in line with the economic recovery," the ministry said. "Moreover, agricultural imports are likely to grow on import deregulation."
Tae Chung, head of research at Jardine Fleming Securities, also echoed the government's caution, pointing out that falling imports of consumer goods kept imports from rising even more.
"Sluggish private consumption is likely to delay a turnaround of the economy," Chung said. "It shows the lack of consumer confidence in economic recovery."
Separately, the consumer price index rose four percent in June on the year, down from a 5.5 percent rise a year earlier, the Ministry of Finance and Economy said.
"The lower CPI would give the government more flexibility to manage money supply, which could boost the economy," Chung said.
